claim: Walking animals must maintain stability in the presence of external perturbations, despite significant temporal delays in neural signaling and muscle actuation.
source: Walking animals must maintain stability in the presence of external perturbations, despite significant temporal delays in neural signaling and muscle actuation.
evidence: This is a general statement about animal locomotion that draws from established scientific understanding.

claim: The presence of significant temporal delays in animal sensorimotor systems establishes fundamental limits on how quickly animals can respond to external perturbations.
source: However, the presence of significant temporal delays in animal sensorimotor systems establishes fundamental limits on how quickly animals can respond to external perturbations (More and Donelan, 2018; Gebehart and Büschges, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to More and Donelan, 2018 and Gebehart and Büschges, 2021.

claim: Sources of temporal delay include neural conduction, synaptic transmission, and electromechanical muscle activation.
source: Sources of temporal delay include neural conduction, synaptic transmission, and electromechanical muscle activation (Sterling, 2015; Ijspeert and Daley, 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sterling, 2015 and Ijspeert and Daley, 2023.

claim: Sensorimotor delays pose a particular challenge for systems that rely on feedback control, because they limit the availability of up-to-date information on the state of the external environment.
source: Sensorimotor delays pose a particular challenge for systems that rely on feedback control, because they limit the availability of up-to-date information on the state of the external environment (Franklin and Wolpert, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Franklin and Wolpert, 2011.

claim: Time delays limit robust performance in feedback control systems.
source: For example, time delays limit robust performance in feedback control systems (Doyle et al., 2013), and model predictive control (MPC) (García et al., 1989; Camacho, 2013; Brunton, 2022) is one algorithmic strategy to improve performance while maintaining robustness.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Doyle et al., 2013.

claim: Model predictive control (MPC) is one algorithmic strategy to improve performance while maintaining robustness in systems with time delays.
source: For example, time delays limit robust performance in feedback control systems (Doyle et al., 2013), and model predictive control (MPC) (García et al., 1989; Camacho, 2013; Brunton, 2022) is one algorithmic strategy to improve performance while maintaining robustness.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to García et al., 1989; Camacho, 2013; Brunton, 2022.

claim: Theoretical studies suggest that some animals use predictive internal models to mitigate the effect of delays.
source: In biological systems, theoretical studies suggest that some animals use predictive internal models to mitigate the effect of delays (More and Donelan, 2018; Li et al., 2023; Desmurget and Grafton, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to More and Donelan, 2018; Li et al., 2023; Desmurget and Grafton, 2000.

claim: Limb compliance and other biomechanical adaptations can compensate for unexpected perturbations within a limited range and mitigate the effect of sensorimotor delays.
source: Limb compliance and other biomechanical adaptations can also compensate for unexpected perturbations within a limited range and mitigate the effect of sensorimotor delays (Daley, 2018; Ashtiani et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Daley, 2018 and Ashtiani et al., 2021.

claim: The constraints that sensorimotor delays impose on robust locomotion have been difficult to quantify, because it is experimentally challenging to manipulate sensorimotor delays and observe their effects on animal locomotion.
source: However, the constraints that sensorimotor delays impose on robust locomotion have been difficult to quantify, because it is experimentally challenging to manipulate sensorimotor delays and observe their effects on animal locomotion (although this has been achieved in other motor systems, for example using focal cooling in singing birds Banerjee et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by the difficulty of experimental manipulation, with a citation to Banerjee et al., 2021 for an example in other motor systems.

claim: Computational models of locomotion typically have not included delays as a tunable parameter, although some models have included them as fixed values.
source: Computational models of locomotion typically have not included delays as a tunable parameter, although some models have included them as fixed values (Geyer and Herr, 2010; Geijtenbeek et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Geyer and Herr, 2010 and Geijtenbeek et al., 2013.

claim: The impact of sensorimotor delays on locomotor control and robustness remains underexplored in computational neuroscience.
source: In general, the impact of sensorimotor delays on locomotor control and robustness remains underexplored in computational neuroscience.
evidence: This is a general assessment of the state of the field based on the authors' review of the literature.

claim: Flies are agile and robust walkers.
source: Flies are agile and robust walkers, and the availability of genetic and behavioral tools in Drosophila makes them well-suited to investigate neural mechanisms of locomotor control (DeAngelis et al., 2019; Gonçalves et al., 2022; Cruz and Chiappe, 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to DeAngelis et al., 2019; Gonçalves et al., 2022; Cruz and Chiappe, 2023.

claim: The availability of genetic and behavioral tools in Drosophila makes them well-suited to investigate neural mechanisms of locomotor control.
source: Flies are agile and robust walkers, and the availability of genetic and behavioral tools in Drosophila makes them well-suited to investigate neural mechanisms of locomotor control (DeAngelis et al., 2019; Gonçalves et al., 2022; Cruz and Chiappe, 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to DeAngelis et al., 2019; Gonçalves et al., 2022; Cruz and Chiappe, 2023.

claim: The fly is the only walking animal whose nervous system is almost completely mapped at synaptic resolution.
source: The fly is also the only walking animal whose nervous system is almost completely mapped at synaptic resolution (Galili et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Galili et al., 2022.

claim: Flies walk rhythmically with a continuum of stepping patterns that range from tetrapod (where two of six legs are off the ground at a time) to tripod (where three of six legs are off the ground at a time).
source: Flies walk rhythmically with a continuum of stepping patterns that range from tetrapod (where two of six legs are off the ground at a time) to tripod (where three of six legs are off the ground at a time) (DeAngelis et al., 2019; Mendes et al., 2013; Szczecinski et al., 2018; Wosnitza et al., 2013; Strauss and Heisenberg, 1990; Nishii, 2000; Pratt et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to DeAngelis et al., 2019; Mendes et al., 2013; Szczecinski et al., 2018; Wosnitza et al., 2013; Strauss and Heisenberg, 1990; Nishii, 2000; Pratt et al., 2024.

claim: Each fly leg has five joints that move through seven mechanical degrees of freedom.
source: Each fly leg has five joints that move through seven mechanical degrees of freedom (Karashchuk et al., 2021; Lobato-Rios et al., 2022) and are actuated by ∼18 muscles that are innervated by ∼70 motor neurons (Azevedo et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Karashchuk et al., 2021 and Lobato-Rios et al., 2022.

claim: Each fly leg is actuated by approximately 18 muscles that are innervated by approximately 70 motor neurons.
source: Each fly leg has five joints that move through seven mechanical degrees of freedom (Karashchuk et al., 2021; Lobato-Rios et al., 2022) and are actuated by ∼18 muscles that are innervated by ∼70 motor neurons (Azevedo et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Azevedo et al., 2024.

claim: Each leg motor neuron is uniquely identifiable.
source: Each leg motor neuron is uniquely identifiable (Azevedo et al., 2024) and receives thousands of synaptic inputs from hundreds of unique premotor neurons within the fly's ventral nerve cord (VNC, Lesser et al., 2024; Cheong et al., 2024), a part of the invertebrate nervous system analogous to the vertebrate spinal cord.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Azevedo et al., 2024.

claim: Each leg motor neuron receives thousands of synaptic inputs from hundreds of unique premotor neurons within the fly's ventral nerve cord (VNC).
source: Each leg motor neuron is uniquely identifiable (Azevedo et al., 2024) and receives thousands of synaptic inputs from hundreds of unique premotor neurons within the fly's ventral nerve cord (VNC, Lesser et al., 2024; Cheong et al., 2024), a part of the invertebrate nervous system analogous to the vertebrate spinal cord.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lesser et al., 2024 and Cheong et al., 2024.

claim: The ventral nerve cord (VNC) is a part of the invertebrate nervous system analogous to the vertebrate spinal cord.
source: Each leg motor neuron is uniquely identifiable (Azevedo et al., 2024) and receives thousands of synaptic inputs from hundreds of unique premotor neurons within the fly's ventral nerve cord (VNC, Lesser et al., 2024; Cheong et al., 2024), a part of the invertebrate nervous system analogous to the vertebrate spinal cord.
evidence: This is established knowledge about invertebrate neuroanatomy.

claim: The first approach to modeling insect multi-legged walking models legs as coupled oscillators or inverted pendula without taking into account the mechanics of leg joints.
source: The first approach models legs as coupled oscillators or inverted pendula without taking into account the mechanics of leg joints. Each leg is a single oscillator, and a network of oscillators is tuned to recreate an oscillatory gait from measurements of footfalls (Couzin-Fuchs et al., 2015; Proctor and Holmes, 2018); alternatively, tripod gaits are approximated by spring-loaded inverted pendula (Chun et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Couzin-Fuchs et al., 2015; Proctor and Holmes, 2018; and Chun et al., 2021.

claim: The second approach to modeling insect multi-legged walking focuses on the physical details of the legs and their joints.
source: The second approach focuses on the physical details of the legs and their joints. Schilling et al., 2013 use a decentralized reactive controller to recreate hexapod walking patterns; Goldsmith, 2019 and Goldsmith et al., 2020 introduce a robotic platform; Lobato-Rios et al., 2022, Wang-Chen et al., 2023, and Vaxenburg et al., 2024 develop virtual fly simulations in a physics engine.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Schilling et al., 2013; Goldsmith, 2019; Goldsmith et al., 2020; Lobato-Rios et al., 2022; Wang-Chen et al., 2023; and Vaxenburg et al., 2024.

claim: Walking behavior in models that focus on physical details of legs is driven by coupled oscillators with tuned parameters that reproduce inter-leg coordination patterns; however, the resultant joint kinematics are typically unrealistic.
source: Walking behavior in these models is also driven by coupled oscillators with tuned parameters that reproduce inter-leg coordination patterns; however, the resultant joint kinematics are typically unrealistic.
evidence: This is an assessment of the models cited in the previous sentence, based on the authors' review.

claim: The third approach to modeling insect multi-legged walking uses normative learning and optimization to generate walking behaviors de novo.
source: The third approach uses normative learning and optimization to generate walking behaviors de novo. Ramdya et al., 2017 maximized fly walking speed by varying inter-leg coordination with a genetic algorithm, whereas (Heess et al., 2017) maximized walking speed in both bipedal and quadruped walkers with reinforcement learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ramdya et al., 2017 and Heess et al., 2017.

claim: Normative models produce walking with varying degrees of realism, but they require a clever selection of objectives with constraints and are computationally expensive.
source: Normative models produce walking with varying degrees of realism, but they require a clever selection of objectives with constraints and are computationally expensive.
evidence: This is an assessment of normative models based on the authors' understanding of the field.

claim: Any change in delay values in normative models would require a computationally intensive retraining process.
source: Furthermore, any change in delay values would require a computationally intensive retraining process.
evidence: This is an inference about the computational requirements of normative models.

claim: Geijtenbeek et al., 2013 include fixed sensorimotor delays in a bipedal model, but do not explore the effect of varying delay values.
source: Notably, Geijtenbeek et al., 2013 include fixed sensorimotor delays in a bipedal model, but do not explore the effect of varying delay values.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Geijtenbeek et al., 2013.

claim: Existing walking models focus on either kinematic or physiological accuracy, but few achieve both, and none consider the effect of varying sensorimotor delays.
source: Overall, existing walking models focus on either kinematic or physiological accuracy, but few achieve both, and none consider the effect of varying sensorimotor delays.
evidence: This is a summary assessment of the state of the field based on the authors' review.

claim: The model is trained on high-resolution 3D joint angle data from walking flies, which has only recently become possible due to new deep learning-based computer vision tools.
source: First, the model is trained on high-resolution 3D joint angle data from walking flies, which has only recently become possible due to new deep learning-based computer vision tools (Karashchuk et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Karashchuk et al., 2021.

claim: The model's multi-layered architecture achieves more than the sum of its parts: specifically, a neural network model recapitulates kinematic coordination of many joints, and an optimal controller allows the data-driven model to generalize to new scenarios (e.g. large delays and perturbations) without retraining.
source: Second, the model's multi-layered architecture achieves more than the sum of its parts: specifically, a neural network model recapitulates kinematic coordination of many joints, and an optimal controller allows the data-driven model to generalize to new scenarios (e.g. large delays and perturbations) without retraining.
evidence: This is a claim about the model's capabilities that will be demonstrated in the Results section.

claim: The model's robustness to perturbations deteriorates when sensorimotor delay parameters exceed the physiological range.
source: However, we found that the model's robustness to perturbations deteriorates when sensorimotor delay parameters exceed the physiological range.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations presented in the Results section.

claim: Fly sensorimotor control circuits operate close to the temporal limit at which they can detect and respond to external perturbations.
source: These results suggest that fly sensorimotor control circuits operate close to the temporal limit at which they can detect and respond to external perturbations.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model results showing that robustness deteriorates beyond physiological delay values.

claim: The model was designed with three functional layers inspired by the hierarchical anatomical organization of the fly nervous system.
source: We designed a walking model with three functional layers (Figure 1B), inspired by the hierarchical anatomical organization of the fly nervous system (Figure 1A, Dallmann et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 1A and 1B, and a citation to Dallmann et al., 2021.

claim: The three layers of the model are an inter-leg phase coordinator, a trajectory generator, and an optimal controller that interfaces with a leg dynamics model.
source: The three layers are an inter-leg phase coordinator, a trajectory generator, and an optimal controller that interfaces with a leg dynamics model.
evidence: This is a description of the model architecture shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Each individual leg is modular and governed by its own dynamics, optimal controller, and trajectory generator.
source: Each individual leg is modular and governed by its own dynamics, optimal controller, and trajectory generator.
evidence: This is a description of the model architecture.

claim: Inter-leg coordination is accomplished by the phase coordinator alone.
source: Inter-leg coordination is accomplished by the phase coordinator alone.
evidence: This is a description of how the model achieves inter-leg coordination.

claim: The movement of each leg is not coupled to any other leg except through the phase of its current step cycle.
source: In other words, the movement of each leg is not coupled to any other leg except through the phase of its current step cycle.
evidence: This is a description of the model's inter-leg coupling mechanism.

claim: The modularity of the model is inspired by the segmental neuroanatomy of the VNC, in which each leg is controlled by distinct local premotor circuits and pools of motor neurons.
source: This modularity is inspired by the segmental neuroanatomy of the VNC, in which each leg is controlled by distinct local premotor circuits and pools of motor neurons (Lesser et al., 2024; Cheong et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lesser et al., 2024 and Cheong et al., 2024.

claim: While the model is inspired by neuroanatomy, its components do not strictly correspond to components of the nervous system.
source: While the model is inspired by neuroanatomy, its components do not strictly correspond to components of the nervous system—the construction of a neuroanatomically accurate model is deferred to future work (see Discussion).
evidence: This is a clarification about the relationship between the model and biological reality.

claim: The model generates 3D walking kinematics that resemble real kinematic data from walking flies.
source: The layered model generates 3D walking kinematics that resemble real kinematic data from walking flies (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 2 showing comparisons between model and data.

claim: In example trajectories of femur-tibia flexion angles of the right front and femur rotation angles of the left middle legs, the simulated time series matched the mean, frequency, and pseudo-triangular shape of the fly data.
source: In example trajectories of femur-tibia flexion angles of the right front and femur rotation angles of the left middle legs, the simulated time series matched the mean, frequency, and pseudo-triangular shape of the fly data (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 2A showing time series comparisons.

claim: The simulated amplitudes were generally smaller than the real amplitudes.
source: For example, the simulated amplitudes were generally smaller than the real amplitudes, and the simulated trajectories tended to be more regular.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing simulated and real data.

claim: The simulated trajectories tended to be more regular than real trajectories.
source: For example, the simulated amplitudes were generally smaller than the real amplitudes, and the simulated trajectories tended to be more regular.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing simulated and real data.

claim: When we averaged joint angles for all legs over 500 distinct walking bouts of 0.5–2 s in duration, we found that the mean differences between real and simulated joint angles were less than 6 degrees.
source: When we averaged joint angles for all legs over 500 distinct walking bouts of 0.5–2 s in duration, we found that the mean differences between real and simulated joint angles were less than 6 degrees (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 2C showing average differences.

claim: The difference between real and simulated joint angles (less than 6 degrees) is comparable to the uncertainty associated with markerless tracking of 3D fly walking kinematics (5.56 degrees).
source: This difference is comparable to the uncertainty associated with markerless tracking of 3D fly walking kinematics that we used as training data (5.56 degrees, from Karashchuk et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim compares the model error to tracking uncertainty from Karashchuk et al., 2021.

claim: The model maintains realistic walking in the presence of external dynamic perturbations, despite being trained only on data of walking without perturbations.
source: Here, we show that our model maintains realistic walking in the presence of external dynamic perturbations, despite being trained only on data of walking without perturbations (no perturbation data was available).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations showing generalization beyond training data.

claim: The combination of the trajectory generator and the optimal controller makes it possible for the model to maintain realistic walking in the presence of external perturbations.
source: This performance is made possible by the combination of the trajectory generator and the optimal controller in the model.
evidence: This is an inference about which model components enable robustness to perturbations.

claim: The optimal controller compensates for external perturbations by taking advantage of proprioceptive feedback, allowing the trajectory generator to sustain realistic joint angle trajectories.
source: Taking advantage of proprioceptive feedback, the optimal controller compensates for external perturbations, allowing the trajectory generator to sustain realistic joint angle trajectories.
evidence: This is an explanation of how the model maintains walking during perturbations.

claim: For both impulse and persistent stochastic perturbations, joint angle trajectories were different during perturbations, but recovered after the perturbation period ended.
source: For both types of perturbation, joint angle trajectories were different during perturbations, but recovered after the perturbation period ended.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation results shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: In the case of persistent stochastic perturbations, kinematics appeared approximately oscillatory even during perturbations, indicating that a semblance of walking was maintained.
source: In the case of persistent stochastic perturbations, kinematics appeared approximately oscillatory even during perturbations, indicating that a semblance of walking was maintained.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation results shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Larger perturbations led to walking behaviors with lower kinematic similarity (KS).
source: As expected, larger perturbations led to walking behaviors with lower KS, and KS was not strongly dependent on forward walking speed (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 4B-C showing KS values across perturbation strengths.

claim: Kinematic similarity (KS) was not strongly dependent on forward walking speed.
source: As expected, larger perturbations led to walking behaviors with lower KS, and KS was not strongly dependent on forward walking speed (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 4B-C showing KS values across walking speeds.

claim: Impulse perturbations appeared to be more challenging for the model than persistent stochastic perturbations, as they resulted in lower kinematic similarity.
source: Impulse perturbations appeared to be more challenging for the model, as they resulted in lower KS.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing the results in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: Impulse perturbations resulted in greater instantaneous deviation from the standard waveform than persistent stochastic perturbations of the same magnitude.
source: From the time series, we observed that impulse perturbations resulted in greater instantaneous deviation from the standard waveform than persistent stochastic perturbations of the same magnitude.
evidence: This is an observation from the time series data in Figure 3.

claim: Impulse perturbations produce simultaneous changes to all legs and joints, whereas persistent stochastic perturbations are spread out in time and typically non-simultaneous.
source: This is due to the fact that impulse perturbations produce simultaneous changes to all legs and joints, whereas persistent stochastic perturbations are spread out in time and typically non-simultaneous.
evidence: This is an explanation of the difference between the two perturbation types based on how they were implemented in the model.

claim: The estimate of sensory delay (5–15 ms) was based on the measured delay from spike initiation in a mechanosensory neuron in the Drosophila femur to the peak of an excitatory postsynaptic potential in a postsynaptic VNC neuron.
source: Our estimate of sensory delay (5–15 ms) was based on the measured delay from spike initiation in a mechanosensory neuron in the Drosophila femur to the peak of an excitatory postsynaptic potential in a postsynaptic VNC neuron (Tuthill and Wilson, 2016b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tuthill and Wilson, 2016b.

claim: The estimate of motor delay (20–40 ms) was based on the time between spike initiation in a tibia motor neuron cell body to the onset of muscle force production, measured with a force probe.
source: Our estimate of motor delay (20–40 ms) was based on the time between spike initiation in a tibia motor neuron cell body to the onset of muscle force production, measured with a force probe (Azevedo et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Azevedo et al., 2020.

claim: Without external perturbations, the model produced realistic walking with arbitrary delays, since the controller can effectively compensate for large delays by using predictions of joint angles in the future.
source: Without external perturbations, the model produced realistic walking with arbitrary delays, since the controller can effectively compensate for large delays by using predictions of joint angles in the future.
evidence: This is an observation about the model's behavior without perturbations.

claim: In the presence of external perturbations and high delay values, the model was unable to maintain realistic walking, since it could not respond rapidly enough to unexpected perturbations.
source: However, in the presence of external perturbations and high delay values, the model was unable to maintain realistic walking, since it could not respond rapidly enough to unexpected perturbations.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation results shown in Figure 5.

claim: For low values of motor delay (10 ms, 20 ms), even stronger perturbations had almost no effect.
source: Examining the time series data, we found that for low values of motor delay (10 ms, 20 ms), even stronger perturbations had almost no effect (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 5A showing time series with different motor delays.

claim: At higher values of motor delay, the effects of the same perturbation became more pronounced, although the model still managed to recover after the perturbations ended.
source: However, at higher values of motor delay, the effects of the same perturbation became more pronounced, although the model still managed to recover after the perturbations ended.
evidence: This is an observation from the time series data in Figure 5A.

claim: The motor delay value of about 30 ms at which the model maintains realistic walking is consistent with motor delays measured from the fruit fly leg, where the time between motor neuron spiking to the onset of muscle force production is about 30 ms.
source: This value is consistent with motor delays measured from the fruit fly leg, where the time between motor neuron spiking to the onset of muscle force production is about 30 ms (Azevedo et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim compares the model result to experimental measurements from Azevedo et al., 2020.

claim: At low values of sensory delay (0 ms, 5 ms), the effects of perturbations on model output were significant.
source: From time series data, we found that even at low values of sensory delay (0 ms, 5 ms), the effects of perturbations on model output were significant (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 5B showing time series with different sensory delays.

claim: When sensory delay increased, the effects of the perturbation became more pronounced.
source: When sensory delay increased, the effects of the perturbation became more pronounced.
evidence: This is an observation from the time series data in Figure 5B.

claim: The sensory delay range of about 10 ms at which the model maintains realistic walking is consistent with experimental estimates of delays from mechanosensory neurons in the fly femur.
source: This range is consistent with experimental estimates of delays from mechanosensory neurons in the fly femur (Tuthill and Wilson, 2016b), although delays could be even longer for more distal sensors.
evidence: This claim compares the model result to experimental measurements from Tuthill and Wilson, 2016b.

claim: Delays could be even longer for more distal sensors, for example, a sensory neuron at the tip of the tarsus would take approximately 20 ms to travel 2 mm at an estimated conduction velocity of approximately 0.3 m/s.
source: For example, a sensory neuron at the tip of the tarsus would take ∼20 ms to travel 2 mm at an estimated conduction velocity of ∼0.3 m/s (Tuthill and Wilson, 2016b).
evidence: This is a calculation based on conduction velocity from Tuthill and Wilson, 2016b.

claim: For any fixed set of values of motor and sensory delays, the kinematic similarity (KS) of perturbed walking was not dependent on forward walking speed.
source: For any fixed set of values of motor and sensory delays, the KS of perturbed walking was not dependent on forward walking speed.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation results shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: Slower walking did not improve the model's ability to sustain walking during perturbations.
source: In other words, slower walking did not improve the model's ability to sustain walking during perturbations (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation results shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: Robust walking was not contingent on the specific values of motor and sensory delay, but rather the sum of these two values.
source: We observed that robust walking was not contingent on the specific values of motor and sensory delay, but rather the sum of these two values (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 5E showing KS values across combinations of motor and sensory delays.

claim: As total delay increased, higher frequencies of walking were impacted first before walking collapsed entirely.
source: Furthermore, as total delay increased, higher frequencies of walking were impacted first before walking collapsed entirely (Appendix 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by results shown in Appendix 9.

claim: In order for the model to overcome a perturbation, the key parameter was the total delay between the perturbation onset and the motor response.
source: Overall, in order for the model to overcome a perturbation, the key parameter was the total delay between the perturbation onset and the motor response.
evidence: This is a summary inference from the simulation results in Figure 5.

claim: The model was able to maintain robust walking only within the physiological range of delay values.
source: When we tested the model across a range of delay values, we found that the model was able to maintain robust walking only within the physiological range.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from Figure 5.

claim: Outside of the physiological range of delays, the model could not maintain walking that was kinematically similar to real flies.
source: Outside of this range, the model could not maintain walking that was kinematically similar to real flies.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from Figure 5.

claim: The fly locomotor control system operates close to the temporal limit at which it can detect and respond to external perturbations.
source: This finding suggests that the fly locomotor control system operates close to the temporal limit at which it can detect and respond to external perturbations.
evidence: This is an inference from the model results showing that robustness is maintained only within physiological delay ranges.

claim: Sensory and motor delays establish a fundamental tradeoff between the speed and robustness of fly walking.
source: Thus, we propose that sensory and motor delays establish a fundamental tradeoff between the speed and robustness of fly walking.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the model results.

claim: The model predicts that at the same perturbation magnitude, walking robustness decreases as delays increase.
source: Our model predicts that at the same perturbation magnitude, walking robustness decreases as delays increase.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model results shown in Figure 5.

claim: This prediction could be experimentally tested by altering conduction velocities on the fly, for example by increasing or decreasing the ambient temperature.
source: This could be experimentally tested by altering conduction velocities on the fly, for example by increasing or decreasing the ambient temperature (Banerjee et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a proposed experimental test with a citation to Banerjee et al., 2021 for a similar approach in another system.

claim: If a warmer ambient temperature decreases delays in the fly, but fly walking robustness remains the same in response to a fixed perturbation, this would indicate a stronger role for central control in walking than the modeling results suggest.
source: If a warmer ambient temperature decreases delays in the fly, but fly walking robustness remains the same in response to a fixed perturbation, this would indicate a stronger role for central control in walking than our modeling results suggest.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of a potential experimental outcome.

claim: It is energetically expensive to build and maintain muscles and neurons that operate with low delay.
source: It is energetically expensive to build and maintain muscles and neurons that operate with low delay (Sterling, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sterling, 2015.

claim: From a performance perspective, long delays limit reaction speed and control robustness, which can ultimately impact animal survival.
source: From a performance perspective, long delays limit reaction speed and control robustness, which can ultimately impact animal survival (More and Donelan, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to More and Donelan, 2018.

claim: In flies, the axons of leg motor neurons and some proprioceptor axons are among the largest diameter cables in the leg nerve, suggesting that the speed of these systems is under selective pressure.
source: In flies, the axons of leg motor neurons and some proprioceptor axons are among the largest diameter cables in the leg nerve (Phelps et al., 2021), suggesting that the speed of these systems is under selective pressure.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Phelps et al., 2021, with an inference about selective pressure.

claim: Fly walking operates in a middle ground with respect to speed and robustness.
source: Our model suggests that fly walking operates in a middle ground with respect to speed and robustness.
evidence: This is an inference from the model results.

claim: The model maintains normal walking for up to about 30 ms of motor delay and 10 ms of sensory delay, which are strikingly close to measured values from Drosophila.
source: Specifically, our model maintains normal walking for up to about 30 ms of motor delay and 10 ms of sensory delay. These values are strikingly close to measured values from Drosophila: 30 ms from motor neuron spike to peak force production in a femur muscle (Azevedo et al., 2020) and 6ms from a femoral mechanosensory neuron spike to the onset of a postsynaptic response in the VNC (Tuthill and Wilson, 2016b).
evidence: This claim compares model results to experimental measurements from Azevedo et al., 2020 and Tuthill and Wilson, 2016b.

claim: In the model, robust locomotion was constrained by the cumulative sensorimotor delay.
source: In our model, robust locomotion was constrained by the cumulative sensorimotor delay.
evidence: This is a summary of the model results from Figure 5E.

claim: This result could be experimentally validated by comparing how animals with different ratios of sensory to motor delays respond to perturbations.
source: This result could be experimentally validated by comparing how animals with different ratios of sensory to motor delays respond to perturbations.
evidence: This is a proposed experimental test of the model prediction.

claim: It may be possible to manipulate sensory vs. motor delays in a single animal, perhaps by altering the development of specific neurons or ensheathing glia.
source: Alternatively, it may be possible to manipulate sensory vs. motor delays in a single animal, perhaps by altering the development of specific neurons or ensheathing glia (Kottmeier et al., 2020).
